look for non-segmental, fluffy, or consolidation-like opacities that spare the central perihilar regions.", "Distinguish from pulmonary edema by confirming the pattern is the 'photographic negative' (peripheral/apical) rather than the classic central/bat-wing distribution.", "Differentiate from organizing pneumonia (which is often patchy, migratory, and less strictly peripheral/apical) and sarcoidosis (which typically presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules rather than peripheral consolidation)."]}, {"category": "classification", "trigger": "When evaluating chest radiographs with interstitial or nodular opacities to determine the underlying etiology based on distribution patterns.", "steps": ["Assess the zonal distribution of opacities by comparing the density of findings in the upper lung zones (apices) versus the lower lung zones (bases).", "Determine the radial distribution by checking if opacities are concentrated along the peribronchovascular bundles and hila (central/perilymphatic) or located in the subpleural regions and outer lung fields (peripheral).", "Classify central/apical predominance as suggestive of sarcoidosis or silicosis, whereas peripheral/apical predominance suggests eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), and basal predominance suggests idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or asbestosis."]}]
